thread.title: All Eyes Are on the Price of Apple’s New iPhones

author: David Marino-Nachison
title: All Eyes Are on the Price of Apple’s New iPhones
text:
Photo: courtesy of Apple By David Marino-Nachison Sept. 13, 2018 10:17 a.m. ET With Wednesday’s Apple (AAPL) event in the rearview mirror , investors are now starting to look ahead—and iPhone prices are what they’re staring at.
As Barron’s Alex Eule noted : “Pushing prices to the max…is the only way Apple is growing iPhone-related sales these days. The new XS Max starts at $1099, making it the most expensive iPhone ever.” On Thursday morning, we scanned Wall Street research to gather impressions.
Guggenheim Partners’ Robert Cihra offered this explanation for why ASPs may be more important than unit volumes:
Newsletter Sign-up “With Apple’s iPhone ASP having increased in 6 of the 10 years since introduction (contrary to typical hardware deflation), those price increases have effectively been a bigger driver of Apple’s revenue ‘upside’ than its units over that period,” Cihra wrote.
• Morgan Stanley ’s Katy Huberty boosted her price target on the shares by $2 to $247, saying “we’re buyers.” She based that on new estimates of 6% year-over-year fiscal 2019 ASP growth; her previous estimate was for a decrease. That, in turn, led her to increase her revenue and EPS forecasts.
“The most significant investor concern entering fiscal 2019 has been that without strong ASP growth, fiscal 2019 iPhone revenue growth is likely to flatline,” she wrote. Yesterday’s news “is likely to dispel that fear.”
• Raymond James’ Chris Caso expects the “midrange [units] for each model to be the most popular—256Gb for the XS and XS Max ($1149/$1249) and 128Gb for the XR ($799). Additionally, we continue to expect the LCD-based XR to represent about 50% of total new device volumes.”
• Will the move help in the long term? KeyBanc Capital Markets’ Andy Hargreaves wondered about that, though he also boosted near-term estimates.
Apple, Hargreaves wrote, is looking to “leverage pricing to extract margin from the least elastic portions of the market. We believe this will largely work through fiscal 2019, but believe it will be challenged in fiscal 2020, unless the company can introduce new features beyond screen size that consumers demand.”
• Maxim Group wondered about the short-term, too, projecting fiscal 2019 ASPs that increase 5% year-over-year.
More About Barron’s Next Learn more about Barron’s Next The Barron’s Next 50 “We still expect Android competition to catch up within mid-fiscal 2019, which we expect will prompt Apple to respond with price cuts beginning with the next iPhone lineup that will be announced in September 2019, and as such we are assuming the ASP decline we had expected in fiscal 2019 gets pushed out to fiscal 2020.”
• New Street Research wrote that the “The $999 XS is as expensive as the X and is therefore unlikely to drive much further trading up and pull-forward we were anticipating (we modeled it at $899),” they wrote. “At the same time, the very good specs of the XR mean this phone could drive some pull-forward and trading up in the low end.”
They expect iPhone revenue to fall 8% in 2019.
• And Nomura Instinet’s Jeffrey Kvaal wondered if the new prices were too high.
“One can fly too close to the sun,” he wrote. “We had expected Apple to restrain ASP increases in fiscal 2019 given underwhelming sales of not only the iPhone X but of Samsung’s nearly $1,000 S and Note models.”
